title: The Hidden Costs of Remote Working

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When offices around the world closed in 2020, many employees discovered, almost by accident, that they could do their jobs just as well from the kitchen table. Years later, remote and hybrid arrangements remain common, and surveys consistently show that most workers who have tried it do not wish to return to a five-day office week. The benefits are well known: no commute, more flexible hours, and fewer distractions from colleagues. What receives far less attention are the costs that remote work quietly shifts from the employer to the employee.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most obvious of these costs is financial. A desk, a chair, a second monitor and a reliable internet connection all cost money, and in most countries employers are under no legal obligation to pay for them. Energy bills also rise when heating or cooling a home office for eight hours a day. A handful of companies offer a fixed monthly stipend to cover such expenses, but surveys suggest that the majority of remote workers receive nothing at all and simply absorb the cost themselves.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second, less visible cost concerns career progression. Several studies tracking promotion rates have found that employees who are rarely seen in the office are, on average, promoted more slowly than colleagues who attend regularly, even when their measurable output is identical. Managers, it seems, continue to associate visibility with commitment, whether or not this reflects actual performance. Remote workers who are new to a company or hoping for rapid advancement may therefore face a disadvantage that has nothing to do with the quality of their work.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The psychological cost is harder to measure but no less real. Without the natural boundary of leaving a building, many remote employees report working longer hours than they did in the office, checking messages late at night and struggling to switch off. At the same time, the absence of casual conversation with colleagues has been linked in several surveys to rising feelings of isolation, particularly among younger workers who are still building a professional network.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: None of this means that remote work is a mistake; for many employees it remains, on balance, a clear improvement over commuting daily to an office. It does suggest, however, that both employers and employees need to treat it as a genuine working arrangement that requires active management, rather than an informal perk that costs nothing. Companies that pay a fair equipment stipend, judge staff by output rather than visibility, and actively protect employees' time outside working hours are likely to keep the benefits of remote work without quietly passing its costs on to their staff.

questions.text: Most employees who have experienced remote work want to return to a full five-day week in the office.
questions.explanation: Đoạn A: "most workers who have tried it do not wish to return to a five-day office week" — ngược với mệnh đề.

questions.text: Employers are legally required to pay for home office equipment in most countries.
questions.explanation: Đoạn B: "in most countries employers are under no legal obligation to pay for them."

questions.text: Most remote workers receive a stipend from their employer to cover home office costs.
questions.explanation: Đoạn B: "the majority of remote workers receive nothing at all and simply absorb the cost themselves."

questions.text: Employees who work remotely are promoted at the same rate as those who regularly attend the office.
questions.explanation: Đoạn C: "employees who are rarely seen in the office are, on average, promoted more slowly... even when their measurable output is identical."

questions.text: Energy bills for a home office are higher in winter than in summer.
questions.explanation: Đoạn B chỉ nói "Energy bills also rise when heating or cooling a home office" — nhắc cả hai trường hợp nhưng không so sánh mùa nào tốn hơn. Không đủ thông tin.

questions.text: According to paragraph C, why might remote workers be promoted more slowly?
options: Their work is measurably worse than that of office-based colleagues
Managers tend to associate being visible in the office with commitment
They are less likely to apply for promotions
They change jobs more often than office-based staff
questions.explanation: Đoạn C: "Managers... continue to associate visibility with commitment, whether or not this reflects actual performance." → B.

questions.text: What does the writer suggest is a common effect of remote work mentioned in paragraph D?
options: Reduced motivation to complete tasks
Difficulty switching off from work in the evening
Increased conflict with managers
A preference for working in noisy environments
questions.explanation: Đoạn D: "checking messages late at night and struggling to switch off." → B.

questions.text: What is the writer's overall conclusion in paragraph E?
options: Remote work should be abandoned because its costs outweigh its benefits
Remote work needs active management so its costs are not quietly shifted onto employees
Employers should require all staff to return to the office
Promotion decisions should depend only on seniority
questions.explanation: Đoạn E: "needs to treat it as a genuine working arrangement that requires active management... without quietly passing its costs on to their staff." → B.

questions.text: Without the natural boundary of leaving a ______, many remote employees work longer hours.
questions.explanation: Đoạn D: "Without the natural boundary of leaving a building."

questions.text: Companies that pay a fair equipment ______ are more likely to keep the benefits of remote work.
questions.explanation: Đoạn E: "Companies that pay a fair equipment stipend... are likely to keep the benefits."

title: Funding the Next Generation of Space Telescopes

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Astronomers have never had so many space telescopes feeding them data, yet many researchers describe themselves as more anxious about the future than at any point in the past two decades. The reason is cost. Each new generation of instruments has proven significantly more expensive than the last, and the flagship missions currently being designed are forecast to cost tens of billions of dollars once construction, launch and operation are included. Agencies that once competed mainly on scientific ambition now compete just as fiercely for a limited pool of public funding.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Part of the problem lies in the nature of the instruments themselves. A telescope designed to detect the faint light of a planet orbiting a distant star must be shielded from its own heat, from sunlight, and from the vibration of its own moving parts, to a degree of precision far beyond that required by earlier missions. Achieving this precision demands new materials and manufacturing techniques that have never been mass-produced, so each component effectively has to be invented before it can be built, driving costs upward long before the telescope ever reaches orbit.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Space agencies have responded in different ways. Some, including NASA, have moved towards international partnerships, splitting both the cost and the credit for a mission across several countries. Others have begun favouring a larger number of smaller, cheaper telescopes over a single enormous flagship, reasoning that the failure of one modest mission is far less damaging, financially and politically, than the failure of a single multi-billion-dollar project. Critics of this approach argue that only the largest telescopes can answer certain fundamental questions, and that spreading funding too thinly risks achieving none of them well.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There is also a growing debate about whether government agencies should remain the primary funders of space science at all. Private companies have dramatically reduced the cost of launching payloads into orbit over the past decade, and a small number of billionaire-funded foundations have begun to finance specific scientific instruments directly. Supporters see this as a welcome source of additional funding; sceptics worry that scientific priorities could increasingly be shaped by the interests of wealthy individuals rather than by the scientific community as a whole.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Whichever funding model eventually dominates, most astronomers agree that public enthusiasm remains essential. Missions that capture the public imagination, as earlier space telescopes have done by returning strikingly detailed images of distant galaxies, tend to find it easier to secure continued funding from governments answerable to taxpayers. For this reason, many scientists now see public communication not as a pleasant addition to their work but as a practical necessity for the survival of the field.

questions.text: Astronomers currently have access to more space telescope data than ever before.
questions.explanation: Đoạn A: "Astronomers have never had so many space telescopes feeding them data."

questions.text: Each new generation of space telescopes has been cheaper than the previous generation.
questions.explanation: Đoạn A: "Each new generation of instruments has proven significantly more expensive than the last."

questions.text: The materials needed for the most advanced telescopes already existed before these missions were designed.
questions.explanation: Đoạn B: "new materials and manufacturing techniques that have never been mass-produced, so each component effectively has to be invented."

questions.text: All space agencies have chosen to build a larger number of smaller telescopes instead of large flagship missions.
questions.explanation: Đoạn C: chỉ "some" chuyển hướng như vậy; "others" vẫn làm khác → không phải "all".

questions.text: Private companies have reduced the cost of launching payloads into orbit.
questions.explanation: Đoạn D: "Private companies have dramatically reduced the cost of launching payloads into orbit."

questions.text: According to paragraph B, what makes building advanced space telescopes particularly expensive?
options: They require precision far beyond that of earlier missions, using untested materials
They must be launched from multiple countries at once
They require far more staff than earlier telescopes
They must operate for a much shorter period of time
questions.explanation: Đoạn B: "precision far beyond that required by earlier missions... new materials... never been mass-produced." → A.

questions.text: What is one criticism of favouring smaller, cheaper telescopes mentioned in paragraph C?
options: They are more likely to fail during launch
They cannot answer certain fundamental scientific questions
They take longer to build than large telescopes
They cost more per telescope than flagship missions
questions.explanation: Đoạn C: "only the largest telescopes can answer certain fundamental questions." → B.

questions.text: What is a concern raised about private funding in paragraph D?
options: It is too small in scale to matter
It may shift scientific priorities towards the interests of wealthy donors
It has made launching payloads more expensive
It is banned in most countries
questions.explanation: Đoạn D: "scientific priorities could increasingly be shaped by the interests of wealthy individuals." → B.

questions.text: To detect the light from a distant planet, a telescope must be shielded from its own ______, from sunlight, and from vibration.
questions.explanation: Đoạn B: "shielded from its own heat, from sunlight, and from the vibration."

questions.text: Many scientists now see public ______ as a practical necessity for the survival of the field.
questions.explanation: Đoạn E: "public communication not as a pleasant addition... but as a practical necessity."

title: The Quiet Rise of Urban Loneliness

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Cities have always been sold as places of connection: more people, more opportunities, more chances to meet like-minded neighbours. Yet a growing body of research suggests that residents of large cities are, on average, more likely to report feeling lonely than people living in smaller towns, a finding that at first seems to contradict common sense. Surveys conducted in several major cities over the past decade have found that around a third of residents report feeling lonely on a regular basis, a proportion notably higher than in rural areas of the same country.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One explanation lies in the nature of urban social contact. City dwellers often interact with dozens of people in a single day, from colleagues to shop assistants to fellow commuters, yet these exchanges are typically brief and impersonal. Researchers distinguish between this kind of passing contact and what they call meaningful social connection, involving people who know one's circumstances and can be relied upon in a crisis. A busy social calendar, it turns out, does not guarantee the second kind of relationship, and some of the loneliest city residents report seeing dozens of people a week.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Housing patterns also play a role. Rising rents in many city centres have pushed young adults towards living alone or moving frequently between short-term rentals, both of which make it harder to build lasting relationships with neighbours. In some cities, the average resident now moves address every two to three years, leaving little time for the kind of familiarity that once developed between people living on the same street over many years.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Technology is frequently blamed, though the evidence here is mixed. Several studies have found no clear link between time spent on social media and loneliness, while others suggest that scrolling through other people's curated lives, particularly when done as a substitute for seeing friends in person rather than alongside it, is associated with greater feelings of isolation. The more consistent finding is that in-person contact with friends, even brief and occasional, correlates strongly with lower loneliness, regardless of how much time a person also spends online.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A number of cities have begun experimenting with responses, from subsidised community centres to redesigned public spaces intended to encourage casual interaction between strangers. Early evaluations suggest modest but genuine benefits, though researchers caution that no single programme is likely to reverse a trend driven by housing costs, working patterns and social habits built up over decades. Addressing urban loneliness, most now agree, will require sustained effort across several areas of city life rather than a single intervention.

questions.text: People living in large cities are, on average, less likely to report loneliness than those in smaller towns.
questions.explanation: Đoạn A: "residents of large cities are, on average, more likely to report feeling lonely than people living in smaller towns."

questions.text: Around a third of city residents in the surveys mentioned report feeling lonely on a regular basis.
questions.explanation: Đoạn A: "around a third of residents report feeling lonely on a regular basis."

questions.text: Seeing a large number of people each week guarantees that a person will not feel lonely.
questions.explanation: Đoạn B: "A busy social calendar... does not guarantee the second kind of relationship, and some of the loneliest city residents report seeing dozens of people a week."

questions.text: Research has found a clear, consistent link between time spent on social media and loneliness.
questions.explanation: Đoạn D: "Several studies have found no clear link between time spent on social media and loneliness."

questions.text: Most people who move into short-term rentals in city centres are under the age of thirty.
questions.explanation: Đoạn C chỉ nói "young adults" chung chung, không nêu độ tuổi cụ thể nào. Không đủ thông tin.

questions.text: What distinction do researchers make in paragraph B?
options: Between lonely people and sociable people
Between brief, impersonal contact and meaningful social connection
Between city life and rural life
Between online friends and offline friends
questions.explanation: Đoạn B: "distinguish between this kind of passing contact and what they call meaningful social connection." → B.

questions.text: According to paragraph C, what effect does moving frequently have?
options: It increases a person's income
It makes it harder to build lasting relationships with neighbours
It reduces rent costs in city centres
It has no effect on social relationships
questions.explanation: Đoạn C: "both of which make it harder to build lasting relationships with neighbours." → B.

questions.text: What does the writer conclude in paragraph E about addressing urban loneliness?
options: A single well-designed programme can solve the problem
It requires sustained effort across several areas of city life
Technology companies should take sole responsibility
The problem cannot be addressed by city governments
questions.explanation: Đoạn E: "will require sustained effort across several areas of city life rather than a single intervention." → B.

questions.text: In some cities, the average resident now moves address every two to three ______.
questions.explanation: Đoạn C: "the average resident now moves address every two to three years."

questions.text: The more consistent finding is that ______ contact with friends correlates strongly with lower loneliness.
questions.explanation: Đoạn D: "in-person contact with friends... correlates strongly with lower loneliness."

title: Electric Vehicles and the Strain on Power Grids

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Sales of electric vehicles have grown rapidly in many countries over the past five years, driven by falling battery prices, government incentives and growing concern about emissions from petrol and diesel engines. Much of the public debate around this shift has focused on the vehicles themselves: their range, their price, and the availability of charging points. Less attention has been paid to a quieter challenge facing the transition, namely whether the electricity grids that will power these vehicles are actually prepared for the additional demand.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The scale of the challenge depends heavily on when vehicles are charged. Electricity grids are generally built with enough spare capacity to handle predictable peaks in demand, such as the early evening period when households return home, turn on lights and begin cooking. If large numbers of electric vehicle owners begin charging their cars at the same time, particularly during this existing peak, the additional load could in theory exceed what local grid infrastructure, especially ageing cables and transformers in older neighbourhoods, was ever designed to carry.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Engineers generally agree that the problem is manageable rather than catastrophic, provided that charging is spread out rather than concentrated. A number of utility companies have introduced time-of-use pricing, charging a lower rate for electricity used overnight when overall demand is low, in the hope of encouraging vehicle owners to delay charging until after the evening peak has passed. Early results suggest that price signals alone can shift a meaningful proportion of charging into off-peak hours, though a significant minority of drivers continue to charge whenever is most convenient, regardless of cost.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more ambitious solution under active development is so-called smart charging, in which a vehicle's charging schedule is automatically managed by the grid operator or the vehicle itself, responding in real time to overall demand across the network. Taken further, some researchers envisage electric vehicles eventually feeding stored energy back into the grid during periods of peak demand, effectively turning millions of parked cars into a distributed battery system. This remains largely experimental, and it would require vehicle owners to accept some loss of control over when their own car charges and discharges.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For now, the consensus among grid planners is that upgrading physical infrastructure, however gradually, remains unavoidable alongside any software-based solution. Many of the cables and transformers serving residential neighbourhoods were installed decades before electric vehicles were a serious consideration, and software can only redistribute demand within the limits that existing hardware allows. The transition to electric transport, in other words, is as much a challenge for electrical engineers quietly working underground as it is for car manufacturers.

questions.text: Public debate about electric vehicles has mainly focused on whether power grids are ready, rather than on the vehicles themselves.
questions.explanation: Đoạn A: "Much of the public debate... has focused on the vehicles themselves... Less attention has been paid to... whether the electricity grids... are actually prepared."

questions.text: If many electric vehicle owners charge their cars at the same time as the existing evening peak, local grid infrastructure could be overloaded.
questions.explanation: Đoạn B: "the additional load could in theory exceed what local grid infrastructure... was ever designed to carry."

questions.text: Time-of-use pricing has completely eliminated charging during peak hours.
questions.explanation: Đoạn C: "a significant minority of drivers continue to charge whenever is most convenient, regardless of cost" — trái với "completely eliminated".

questions.text: Technology that lets electric vehicles feed energy back into the grid is already in widespread commercial use.
questions.explanation: Đoạn D: "This remains largely experimental."

questions.text: Government incentives for electric vehicles vary significantly between countries.
questions.explanation: Đoạn A chỉ nhắc "government incentives" là một nguyên nhân chung, không so sánh mức độ giữa các nước. Không đủ thông tin.

questions.text: According to paragraph C, what approach have utility companies used to influence when EVs are charged?
options: Banning charging during the evening peak
Offering a lower electricity rate overnight
Limiting the number of vehicles each household may own
Subsidising the purchase of larger batteries
questions.explanation: Đoạn C: "time-of-use pricing, charging a lower rate for electricity used overnight." → B.

questions.text: What is described as a more ambitious solution in paragraph D?
options: Building entirely new power stations
Smart charging that responds automatically to demand across the network
Banning electric vehicles from charging at home
Reducing the number of electric vehicles sold each year
questions.explanation: Đoạn D: "smart charging, in which a vehicle's charging schedule is automatically managed... responding in real time to overall demand." → B.

questions.text: What is the writer's main point in paragraph E?
options: Software solutions alone are sufficient to solve the grid problem
Physical infrastructure upgrades remain necessary alongside software solutions
Electric vehicles should be banned until infrastructure improves
Car manufacturers bear sole responsibility for the problem
questions.explanation: Đoạn E: "upgrading physical infrastructure... remains unavoidable alongside any software-based solution." → B.

questions.text: Engineers generally agree the problem is manageable, provided that charging is spread out rather than ______.
questions.explanation: Đoạn C: "provided that charging is spread out rather than concentrated."

questions.text: Some researchers envisage electric vehicles turning millions of parked cars into a distributed ______ system.
questions.explanation: Đoạn D: "turning millions of parked cars into a distributed battery system."
